# 查询隐含式GEO：从文档本身找到应补充的信息

英文题名：*Query Implied Generative Engine Optimization*。作者：Shilpa Ramakrishna、William B. Andreopoulos，圣何塞州立大学计算机科学系。本稿译自本地八页PDF，覆盖全部正文、八个公式、四张表、五幅图及结论；书目在末尾逐页英文中保留。原文页边同时写arXiv:2609.27845v1与“19 Aug 2026”，日期标记存在不一致，本稿不擅改。

> 最值得先理解的一点：作者不用用户问题来改写文档，但评估时仍需要查询。它在固定的五篇候选文档中测试“生成器会不会更多引用”，没有实测改写后网页能否更容易进入搜索候选。

## 第一部分：完整中文译文

### 摘要

在线信息搜索的格局已显著改变。生成式搜索引擎（GSE）使用大语言模型为查询生成自然语言回答，内容创作者的可见性不再只由搜索排名决定，还取决于是否被生成回答引用。但GSE是黑箱，由此产生了旨在提高可见性的生成式引擎优化（GEO）。多数现有方法依赖明确查询或从查询派生的信号，使内容更符合用户需求。

我们提出查询隐含式生成引擎优化QI-GEO，直接从文档推断用户意图。它近似文档相关意图空间，识别尚缺失但可能帮助回答潜在问题的内容。在GEO-Bench和Extended GEO-Bench上的评估显示，客观评分最高提高15.9%，主观评分最高17.6%，新增引用约为丢失引用的两倍。结果表明，不依赖显式查询输入、从文档近似用户意图，也能改善可见性。

关键词：GEO、知识图谱、意图推断、自然语言处理、内容可见性。

### I 引言

二十多年来，Google、Yahoo等以关键词检索和搜索结果页列表作为主要信息入口，创作者用SEO改善排名。LLM催生GSE：检索相关来源，综合成连贯自然语言回答，经常附来源引用。用户越来越常问完整问题，而非输入关键词；可见性因此既与检索排名有关，也与是否被选入生成回答有关。仅靠传统SEO可能不足。

GEO为此提出，旨在增加文档被引用概率。奠基工作定义生成输出可见性，以及客观、主观印象指标，并证明简单内容改动也能产生影响。RAID、C-SEO、IF-GEO继续探索替代策略，但多数依赖明确查询或查询信号。创作者通常不知道用户会问一个主题的全部问题，黑箱环境下这种依赖很难满足。

查询经常是用户意图的代理。QI-GEO转而从文档推断意图：文档的实体和关系表达语义，也反映读者可能关心的信息。将这些关系结构化，再借外部知识扩展，可以近似文档周围的更广语义空间，无须生成查询。

扩展时会出现与主题密切相关却未被明确介绍的概念。这些是潜在信息缺口，可能限制文档满足多种需求的能力。QI-GEO识别并补入缺失信息，以文档语义结构而非生成问题作为优化依据，试图形成更稳定的意图表征并提升未见问题下的可见性。

贡献有二：提出直接由文档语义推断潜在意图、无需显式查询的QI-GEO；在GEO-Bench和ExtendedGEOBench用客观、主观、引用及稳定性指标评估，覆盖单查询和多查询条件。

### II 相关工作

多数GEO研究采用固定检索：某查询的候选文档池保持不变，隔离内容改动与检索波动，成为方法比较常见协议。

**A GEO。** 基础工作表明增加引用、统计、权威资料等内容改动可影响可见性。方法从规则改写发展到意图感知、多查询优化。RAID借意图推断和结构化计划对齐需求，IF-GEO以先发散再收敛覆盖多个相关问题，C-SEO等提出其他策略与评估。但通常仍使用显式或派生查询。

**B 查询与意图。** 早期方法针对已知查询，后续生成相关问题/变体近似广泛意图。RAID还用用户角色模拟与反思，IF-GEO用反向检索生成潜在问题。它们表达不同，通常都把查询作为近似需求的主要手段。

**C 评估框架与指标。** GEO-Bench含10,000个跨领域、跨来源查询。RAID扩展成按语义相关查询分组的ExtendedGEOBench，支持稳健性及多查询评估，IF-GEO也用此研究一致性。指标包括字数、位置加权字数PAWC，G-EVAL等LLM评委主观指标，以及最坏表现、下行风险、赢/平率。由于创作者难掌握完整查询空间，仍需文档中心的意图推断，构成本研究动机。

### III 问题形式化

GSE为查询q检索候选集合Cq，然后生成：

$$r_q=Generate(q,C_q).\tag{1}$$

可见性v(D,q)描述文档D对q在生成回答中的引用贡献、位置或主观影响。优化方法M生成D′=M(D)，每问题增益：

$$\Delta v_i=v(D',q_i)-v(D,q_i).\tag{2}$$

文档需要覆盖多个相关问题Q(D)，整体效果聚合为：

$$\Delta=\mathcal A(\{\Delta v_i\}_{i=1}^{m}).\tag{3}$$

聚合算子可为均值或最小值。相关查询通常被假设已知或能生成，但实际查询分布P(D)未知。目标是：

$$\max_M\mathbb E_{q\sim P(D)}[v(M(D),q)-v(D,q)].\tag{4}$$

既然优化时P(D)不可得，就需要从文档直接得到替代意图表征。下一节用语义扩展完成此事。

### IV 方法

#### A QI-GEO概览

QI-GEO不针对已知或生成查询改写，而从实体与关系推断潜在需求。流程先提取语义关系并链接到知识图谱，再扩展相关概念、建立已有覆盖图，按主题相关性排序候选缺口，把最值得补的转为定向编辑，同时保持原文内容与结构。

图1显示原文→关系挖掘→Wikidata图谱链接与扩展，同时生成覆盖图→汇聚评分与top-K选择→判断是否有有效缺口；有则交文档改写器，没有则图中进入“Fallback：LLM rewrite”；原文与优化文档分别配同一个固定检索池，在查询驱动的评估引擎中比较。图示回退分支在方法正文没有详细参数说明。

![[附件_57/原文第4页.png]]

#### B 关系挖掘与知识图谱构建

先对全文做指代消解，把代词和其他指代表达替换成对应实体，减少歧义，保留跨句关系，避免提取残缺关系。然后关系提取模型将文本变成“主语—关系—宾语”三元组。三元组紧凑地表示语义，并兼容知识图谱实体和关系。

再将实体与关系链接到图谱标识，置于共享语义空间，为扩展提供一致表示。所有已链接三元组组成文档知识图谱，是后续管线基础。

#### C 知识扩展与覆盖映射

对每个已链接实体检索一跳邻居。限制一跳，是为了保留与原主题直接相连的概念，减少无关内容，并使每个缺口都能解释为原文实体的一步语义延伸。进一步过滤主要表达元数据、导航的关系，优先定义、因果和解释关系。

同时建立覆盖图，记录原文已经表达的实体—关系对，以区分真缺口与已有信息。扩展发现但覆盖图中没有的概念，作为候选缺口送入下一步排序。

#### D 缺口发现与排序

扩展通常产生大量弱相关概念，需要同时满足“文档强烈隐含”与“确实尚未介绍”。QI-GEO用汇聚评分：若多个文档实体独立支持同一候选，比单一来源支持更可能是真正需求。

先按语义功能给关系分组，如定义、因果、机制、元数据，防止语义近似关系分散证据。各关系组赋“侧面权重”，反映对读者内容的价值，通常定义和解释高于导航、元数据。

$$S_{struct}=conv(g,d)\times w_{facet}(g)\times c_{src}(e).\tag{5}$$

g为关系组，conv为汇聚程度，w为该组权重，c为源实体重要性。汇聚定义为独立支持候选关系组的不同文档实体数量：

$$conv(g,d)=|\{e\in E_d:\exists\ candidate\ (g,n)\ from\ e\}|.\tag{6}$$

源实体重要性以提及频次归一化：

$$c_{src}(e)=\frac{count(e,d)}{\max_{e'\in E_d}count(e',d)}.\tag{7}$$

文档中心实体有更大作用，偶尔提及的实体作用较小。评分后做两轮覆盖检查：精确检查移除已存在的实体—关系对；语义检查识别同义表达，移除其实已经讲过的信息。通过两轮的才视为真缺口，按分数选最高者改写。

#### E 文档改写

不是自由重写全文，而是给出结构化编辑规格，包含锚点、建议、必要性分数。锚点指最相关句段，建议描述待加入概念，必要性反映补充重要程度。锚定已有内容，让修改位置明确并符合上下文。

编辑按顺序作用于当前版本，要求局部增加、避免大改。多数情况下，仅在锚点追加短分句或一句话，保留其余内容。每次修订都能追溯具体缺口和原位置，便于检查验证。最终文档增加高价值缺失信息，同时保留原意、结构和内容。

### V 实验结果：设计

#### A 研究问题

RQ1：没有显式用户查询，能否直接从文档推断意图？RQ2：语义扩展能否发现相关缺失信息并改善生成搜索可见性？RQ3：这种查询无关优化，面对同一需求的不同说法是否一致有效？

#### B 数据集

GEO-Bench包含10,000查询—文档实例，领域多样。每查询固定五篇候选，指定一篇优化目标。ExtendedGEOBench将同一需求的不同说法分组，检验是否不局限一个查询。

所有实验固定候选池，保持其他文档不变，只把目标的原版换为QI-GEO版本；作者意在把可见性变化归于内容修改，排除检索变化。

#### C 配置

管线结合关系提取、图谱扩展、LLM改写。比较REBEL、RELiK、spaCy、Qwen2.5提取器；报告结果均使用REBEL，因为它持续产生最适合扩展的三元组，其关系词汇与图谱属性自然对齐，使链接与扩展更可靠。

三元组链接图谱，取一跳邻居，过滤通用及元数据关系，保留定义、解释、因果；按汇聚评分并做相似度及覆盖检查。选中缺口转为编辑请求，由Qwen2.5 7B在原文锚点局部添加，不显著改变结构和含义。

#### D 评估指标

客观指标WC表示生成内容归于该文档的比例；PI表示引用位置的突出程度；PAWC结合二者，早出现贡献权重更高，作为主要客观指标。原文公式排版为：

$$Imp_{pwc}(c_i,r)=\frac{\sum_{s\in S_{c_i}}|s|\,e^{-pos(s)/|S|}}{\sum_{s\in S_r}|s|}.\tag{8}$$

$S_{c_i}$为引用文档ci的句子，Sr为全部回答句子。若一句多引，贡献均分给各来源。原文公式符号|S|与正文Sr略有记法差异，按原排版保留，不把它误读为指数外再除。

主观印象用LLM评委，从相关性、影响力、独特性、多样性、点击追随可能性、主观位置、主观体量七维分别五分打分，再平均。

稳定性包括：Mean Gain平均相对改善；WTR优化后至少不差的查询比例；WCP所有查询中最大下降；DR负结果的程度。它们补充均值，反映失败风险。

### VI 结果与讨论

除另说明，比较原文与优化版，检索池和评估条件不变。

#### A 引用覆盖

|表I：被引用比例|原文|QI-GEO|绝对变化|相对变化|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|单查询|.657|.726|+.069|+10.5%|
|多查询×5|.713|.772|+.059|+8.3%|

单查询从.657到.726，相对+10.5%。原文接着解释为“此前被生成器忽略的文档大约十分之一在优化后被引用”；这句话与表格分母不完全相符，译后详细校读。多查询同样正向，幅度稍小。

图2列引用状态翻转：单查询（图标400w）新增123、丢失55，约2.2倍、净增68；多查询×5新增616、丢失323，约1.9倍、净增293。新增明显多于丢失，作者据此认为覆盖增加不是少数大改善驱动，而是更多目标获得引用。

![[附件_57/原文第6页.png]]

#### B 来源可见性

文档除了被引用，还要贡献内容，因此比较PAWC：

|表II：平均Wordpos/PAWC|原文|QI-GEO|绝对变化|相对变化|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|单查询|.2137|.2407|+.0270|+12.6%|
|多查询×5|.2038|.2363|+.0325|+15.9%|

作者认为优化文档不但引用更多，也倾向更早出现、贡献更多内容。并非每查询改善，但整体分布偏正，均值在两条件均正。客观WTR=.70，约七成不差于原版；DR=.011，作者将其解释为负面影响通常较小，整体在大量查询上稳健。

#### C 主观评估

LLM评委对七维评分：

|表III：平均主观分|原文|QI-GEO|绝对变化|相对变化|
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|单查询|2.332|2.743|+.411|+17.6%|
|多查询×5|2.137|2.503|+.366|+17.1%|

客观改善也反映在评委感知的有用程度与突出程度。图3、4显示低分比例下降、中高分增加：单查询1—5分桶分别变化−17.9%、+5.7%、+8.4%、+3.8%、+0.0%；多查询为−15.4%、+9.1%、+4.4%、+1.9%、+0.0%。图轴为查询比例变化，即百分点。作者认为主要是弱可见性文档移向中高可见性。

主观WTR=.81，即超过五分之四查询得分不降；仍有负结果，但整体偏正。因此改善不限引用统计，也表现在评委认为更相关、更有影响和更可见。

#### D 多查询稳健性

ExtendedGEOBench每文档五个语义近似问题，以文档为单位聚合，而非独立分析每个查询。

|表IV：每文档多查询稳定性|值|
|---|---:|
|五种说法平均增益非负（原表写net-positive且≥0）|66.0%|
|至少3/5说法改善或持平|73.7%|
|全部五种说法改善或持平，≥0|22.2%|
|有帮助时平均增益|+.1634|
|有损害时平均损失|−.0629|
|WTR：每文档获益说法比例的平均|.67|
|DR：每文档下行风险的平均|.0097|

作者认为66%文档平均正向，73.7%多数说法不降，22.2%五种都不降，说明改善一般能跨越单一说法。获益时平均幅度大于损失，DR低，负面幅度相对有限。

图5按最佳查询增益排序每文档，画最坏WCP到最好BCP区间。87.5%文档至少一种说法获益；平均BCP=+.2070，平均WCP=−.1328。多数文档至少一条说法受益明显，但不同说法差异存在。作者据此认为文档中心意图表征能跨查询措辞泛化。

![[附件_57/原文第7页.png]]

### VII 结论与未来工作

QI-GEO不依赖显式或派生查询，而直接从文档提取实体关系，经图谱扩展找信息缺口，在未知未来查询时发现可能有用的概念。两基准上改善引用覆盖、来源可见性和主观印象，并跨相关问题保持效果，支持文档中心意图作为替代方案。

未来可用更丰富图谱扩展提升缺口质量及覆盖；联合建模多个推断意图，而非独立处理各缺口；当前为通用图谱，未来领域图谱可为法律、金融、医疗、地理空间等提供更精准关系。以上有望提升查询无关GEO的效果与泛化。

## 第二部分：逐章详细讲解与练习

### I—III：不知道用户会怎么问，也可以先检查文章漏了什么

这篇不是让你忽略真实客户问题。它解决的是“只有一篇现有稿，没有完整搜索词库”的情形。例子：文章介绍“家庭光纤宽带”，已写光纤、路由器、带宽，却没解释光猫、Wi-Fi覆盖、上下行区别。用户未必用你写的标题提问，补齐真正相关缺口可能让文章支持更多问法。

意图仍是推断，不是真实用户调查。一个概念在图谱里有关联，不代表读者此刻需要；必须人工判断它是否服务原文目标。更不能因为“相关”就把所有邻居写进去。

式2教学例子：一问题原PAWC=.20，优化=.25，绝对增益=.05，相对增益25%。另问题原.40、优化.38，绝对−.02，相对−5%。绝对平均(.05−.02)/2=.015，相对平均(25%−5%)/2=10%；先求平均再算相对变化又是(.315−.30)/.30=5%。这三者不能混称同一个Mean Gain。

练习：挑一篇自己旧稿，写下目标读者、要完成的任务、不打算覆盖的范围，再找缺口。这样图谱扩展不会把文档写成百科。

### IV-B：把文章拆成三元组

例句：“路由器连接光猫，它把网络分给多台设备。”先确定“它”指路由器，再拆为“路由器—连接—光猫”“路由器—分发网络给—终端设备”。若错误消解为光猫，后续会沿错误实体扩展。

实体链接不是把词抄进表格，而是确定所指对象。例如“苹果”是水果还是公司；“光猫”对应光网络终端而非普通路由器。链接错误会导致一整串无关补充。

练习表：原句、实体、关系、对象、原文证据位置、是否有歧义。先手工做十条足够，不必初学就安装知识图谱系统。本文最终用REBEL，但没有说任何行业REBEL都最好。

### IV-E：锚点编辑怎么写？

原句：“选择路由器时要关注无线速率。”候选缺口是“实际体验受终端能力和环境影响”。教学编辑卡：锚点=该句；建议=解释标称速率不等于实际下载速率，并检查终端协议与环境；必要性=高；依据=设备文档及适用条件。改成：“选择路由器时要关注无线速率，同时核对终端支持的标准和使用环境；标称无线连接速率不等于实际下载速率。”

这是一处有边界的补充。不要改成“购买本品牌路由器就能提升AI推荐”之类不相关宣传，也不要编数字。每次编辑都记录新增事实来源和版本，避免后续修改冲突。

### V：固定检索到底控制了什么？

想象考试给模型固定五份资料，你只改其中一份，看模型答案是否更使用它。这样测的是“已经进入候选后的内容竞争”，不是“整个互联网上它能否被搜到”。网页上线、索引、抓取、检索排名都未在此实验中检验。

PAWC教学算例：回答四句，每句20词，共80词；目标文档被第1、3句引用，假设位置从1计、每句独引。分子20e^(−1/4)+20e^(−3/4)≈25.02，除80约.313。若第1句同时引两来源，把它对目标的20词贡献减半，约(.5×15.58+9.45)/80=.215。这里位置计数等是明示教学假设，原文未把所有实现细节写齐。

七维主观分是LLM判断，不是七组真人满意度；“点击追随可能性”也是评分项，不是实测点击率。练习时把人工依据另存，别只信一个综合分。

引用覆盖从65.7%到72.6%，是增加6.9个百分点，相对增长10.5%。若没有原始转移表，不能据此得出“原来没引用的10.5%被救回”。图2提供的是新增123、丢失55、净增68；与原未引分母配合才可算转化比例，且需要确切样本量。

### VII：最小可落地流程

先选已有文章，确定任务边界；抽十条实体关系；找一跳邻近且有可靠出处的候选；删掉已有同义信息和跑题关系；用汇聚直觉挑三条；做局部锚点编辑；在五种问法下检查是否更完整、有无新错误；保存原稿、修改版、编辑卡和评估表。无需付费工具也能先完成手工版。

完成标准不是“写得更长”，而是每个新增句都能回答一个原稿不能充分回答的合理信息需要，并可核验。QI-GEO论文启发此流程，但没有证明手工版会得到同样15.9%提升。

```text
Abstract—The landscape of search has changed drastically
with how people look for information online. Traditional search
engines are being replaced by Generative Search Engines (GSEs),
which use Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate natural
language responses to user queries. For content creators, visibility
is no longer solely determined by ranking in search results but by
being cited within generated responses. But Generative Search
Engines are black-boxes, leading to the emergence of Generative
Engine Optimization (GEO), a set of techniques aimed at improv-
ing content visibility in generative search settings. Most existing
approaches rely on the explicit queries or query derived signals
to align content to better suit user needs. We propose Query
Implied Generative Engine Optimization (QI-GEO) to infers user
intent directly from the document. Our approach approximates
document’s intent space and identifies content that may be
missing yet relevant to answer potential user queries. Evalu-
ation on GEO-Bench and Extended GEO-Bench demonstrated
improvements across objective and subjective metrics. QI-GEO
improved objective scores by up to 15.9% and subjective scores
by up to 17.6%, while yielding nearly twice as many citation gains
as citation losses. These results suggest that document-derived
approximations of user intents can improve visibility without
relying on explicit query inputs.

I. INTRODUCTION
For more than twenty years, search engines such as Google,
Yahoo, and others have been the primary means for people
to find information online. These systems relied on keyword-
based retrieval and returned ranked lists of websites known
as Search Engine Results Pages (SERPs). Content creators
used Search Engine Optimization (SEO) techniques to improve
rankings and increase visibility within these results. With
the introduction of Large Language Models (LLMs), a new
type of search system emerged: Generative Search Engines
(GSEs) [1]. Unlike traditional search engines, GSEs generate
natural language answers by retrieving relevant sources and
synthesizing information into a coherent response [2]. These
responses often include citations to the sources used during
generation [3]. As users increasingly interact with search
systems through complete questions rather than keywords,
visibility now depends not only on ranking in search results but
also on being selected and cited within generated answers [4].
As a result, traditional SEO practices alone may be insufficient
to maintain visibility.
To address visibility in generative search environments,
the concept of Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) was
introduced [5]. GEO refers to a set of techniques designed
to increase the likelihood that a document will be cited in
responses generated by GSEs. The foundational GEO work
introduced the concept of visibility in generative outputs
and proposed objective and subjective impression metrics for
evaluating it [5]. It also demonstrated that even simple content
modifications can significantly affect visibility. Subsequent
approaches such as RAID [6], C-SEO [7], and IF-GEO [8]
further explored GEO and proposed alternative optimization
strategies. However, most existing methods rely on explicit
queries or query-derived signals to guide optimization. In
practice, content creators rarely know the full range of ques-
tions users may ask about a topic, making query-dependent
optimization difficult in black-box generative search systems.
Queries are often used as a proxy for user intent. In this
work, we propose Query-Implied Optimization (QI-GEO), a
framework that seeks to infer user intent directly from the
document rather than relying on explicit query inputs. The key
idea behind QI-GEO is that documents contain entities and re-
lationships that capture their underlying semantics and reflect
the information users may be interested in. By representing
these relationships in a structured form and expanding them
using external knowledge, QI-GEO approximates the broader
semantic space surrounding a document without requiring
query generation.
During this expansion process, concepts emerge that are
closely related to the document’s topic but are not explicitly
covered in its content. These concepts can be viewed as po-
tential informational gaps that may limit a document’s ability
to address diverse user information needs. QI-GEO leverages
these gaps as opportunities for optimization. By identifying
and incorporating relevant missing information, QI-GEO im-
proves content coverage while grounding optimization in the
document’s semantic structure rather than generated queries.
This provides a more stable representation of user intent and
helps improve visibility across unseen queries.
In summary, the contributions of this work are as follows.
First, we propose Query-Implied Optimization (QI-GEO), a
GEO framework that infers latent user intent directly from
document semantics without relying on explicit query inputs.
Second, we evaluate QI-GEO on GEO-Bench and Extended-
GEOBench using objective, subjective, citation-based, and sta-
```

```text
II. RELATED WORKS
Most GEO research assumes a fixed-retrieval setting, where
the candidate document pool associated with a query remains
constant throughout evaluation [5], [6], [8]. This setup isolates
the effect of content modifications from retrieval variability
and has become the standard evaluation protocol for compar-
ing GEO methods [5], [6], [8].
A. Generative Engine Optimization
Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) was introduced as
a set of techniques for improving document visibility in
generated responses [5]. The foundational GEO work proposed
objective and subjective visibility metrics and demonstrated
that content modifications such as adding citations, statistics,
and authoritative references can significantly improve visibil-
ity. Subsequent works such as RAID [6], IF-GEO [8], and
C-SEO [7] extended GEO through alternative optimization
strategies and evaluation frameworks.
GEO methods have evolved from rule-based rewriting to
intent-aware and multi-query optimization. RAID uses intent
inference and structured rewriting plans to better align content
with user information needs [6], while IF-GEO focuses on
optimizing documents across multiple related queries through
a diverge-then-converge framework [8]. Despite these differ-
ences, most GEO approaches rely on explicit queries or query-
derived signals to guide optimization.
B. Query and Intent Modeling
User intent is a central component of GEO because visibility
depends on how well a document aligns with user information
needs. Early GEO approaches optimize content with respect
to known queries [5]. More recent methods generate related
queries or query variants to approximate a broader intent space
[6], [8].
RAID further models intent through user-role simulation
and reflection mechanisms [6], while IF-GEO employs reverse
retrieval to generate potential queries for a document [8].
Although these methods differ in how intent is represented,
they generally treat queries as the primary mechanism for
approximating user needs.
C. Evaluation Frameworks and Metrics
GEO-Bench is the most widely used benchmark for eval-
uating GEO methods and contains 10,000 queries spanning
diverse domains and query sources [5]. RAID extends this
benchmark through ExtendedGEOBench, which groups se-
mantically related queries to support robustness and multi-
query evaluation [6]. IF-GEO further uses this setting to study
optimization consistency across related queries [8].
Existing work evaluates visibility using objective metrics
such as Word Count and Position-Adjusted Word Count
(PAWC) [5], subjective metrics based on LLM-as-a-judge
approaches such as G-EVAL [9], and stability metrics such as
Worst-Case Performance, Downside Risk, and Win-Tie Rate
[8].
Existing GEO methods have progressed from rule-based
rewriting to intent-aware and multi-query optimization. How-
ever, most approaches model user intent through explicit
queries, generated queries, or query-derived signals. Since
content creators rarely know the complete space of possible
user queries, there remains a need for methods that can infer
intent directly from the document itself. This gap motivates
the document-centric approach explored in this work.
```

```text
IV. METHODOLOGY
A. Overview of QI-GEO
Query-Implied Optimization (QI-GEO) is a document-
centric GEO framework that improves visibility in generative
search engines without relying on explicit query inputs. Instead
of optimizing content for known or generated queries, QI-
GEO attempts to infer user intent directly from the document’s
semantic structure. The central idea is that entities and rela-
tionships present in a document reflect the information needs
associated with its topic. By expanding these relationships
using external knowledge, QI-GEO approximates the broader
semantic space surrounding the document and identifies con-
cepts that are relevant but not explicitly covered.
Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow of QI-GEO. The
framework first extracts semantic relationships from the doc-
ument and grounds them in a knowledge graph. The resulting
graph is then expanded to discover related concepts and
construct a coverage map of the document’s existing semantic
content. Candidate informational gaps are ranked according
to their relevance to the document’s topic, and the most
promising gaps are converted into targeted edits. These edits
are incorporated into the document to improve coverage of
potential user information needs while preserving the original
content and structure.
B. Relation Mining and Knowledge Graph Construction
QI-GEO begins by converting the document into a struc-
tured semantic representation that can be expanded and ana-
lyzed. Since the framework models intent through entities and
their relationships, the first step is to identify the key concepts
discussed in the document and how they are connected.
To reduce ambiguity, coreference resolution is first applied
to the entire document so that pronouns and other referring
expressions are replaced with their corresponding entities.
This preserves semantic relationships that span multiple sen-
tences and prevents incomplete relations from being extracted.
The resolved document is then processed using a relation
extraction model, which converts text into a collection of
subject–relation–object triplets. Each triplet captures a seman-
tic relationship expressed in the document and serves as the
interface between unstructured text and structured knowledge.
Triplets are used because they provide a compact representa-
tion of document semantics while remaining compatible with
knowledge graph entities and relations.
The extracted entities and relations are subsequently linked
to identifiers in a knowledge graph. Entity linking grounds
document concepts in a shared semantic space and pro-
vides a consistent representation for downstream expansion.
The resulting grounded triplets collectively form a document
knowledge graph that serves as the semantic foundation for
the remainder of the QI-GEO pipeline.
C. Knowledge Expansion and Coverage Mapping
Once the document graph has been constructed, QI-GEO
expands it to explore information related to the document’s
topic. The objective of this stage is to approximate the broader
semantic space surrounding the document and identify con-
cepts that may be relevant to potential user information needs.
Rather than generating possible queries, QI-GEO explores
concepts that are semantically connected to the document
through a knowledge graph.
For each linked entity, QI-GEO retrieves neighboring con-
cepts using one-hop expansion. Restricting expansion to im-
mediate neighbors keeps the process focused on concepts
that are directly related to the document and reduces the
introduction of unrelated information. This also makes the
resulting gaps easier to justify, since every candidate remains
only one semantic step away from concepts already present
in the document. To further improve relevance, relation types
that primarily encode metadata or navigational information
are filtered, while relations that capture definitional, causal,
or explanatory information are prioritized.
Alongside expansion, QI-GEO builds a coverage map that
records the entity–relation pairs already expressed in the
document. The purpose of the coverage map is to distinguish
genuinely missing concepts from information that is already
present. Concepts discovered during expansion that are not
represented in the coverage map are treated as candidate
informational gaps. These candidates are passed to the next
stage, where they are evaluated and ranked according to their
relevance to the document.
D. Gap Discovery and Ranking
Knowledge graph expansion typically produces a large
number of candidate concepts, many of which are only weakly
related to the document. The objective of this stage is to iden-
tify concepts that are both strongly implied by the document
and genuinely absent from its content.
QI-GEO ranks candidate concepts using a convergence-
based scoring strategy. The intuition is that concepts inde-
pendently supported by multiple entities in the document are
more likely to represent meaningful informational gaps than
concepts originating from a single source. A candidate concept
that is repeatedly implied by different parts of the document
provides stronger evidence of an underlying information need
and is therefore assigned higher importance.
To prevent semantically similar relations from fragmenting
evidence, relation properties are first grouped according to
their semantic function. Examples include definitional, causal,
mechanistic, and metadata-oriented relations. Each relation
group is assigned a facet weight that reflects its usefulness for
reader-facing content. Definitional and explanatory relations
are generally assigned higher weights than navigational or
metadata relations.
The structural score of a candidate concept is computed as:
```

```text
After scoring, candidate concepts are evaluated against the
coverage map. Exact coverage checks remove concepts whose
entity–relation pairs already exist in the document. A second
semantic coverage check compares candidate concepts against
document content to identify information that is already ex-
pressed using different wording. Candidates that pass both
checks are treated as true informational gaps.
The remaining gaps are ranked according to their scores,
and the highest-ranked candidates are selected for document
rewriting.
E. Document Rewriting
The final stage of QI-GEO converts the selected infor-
mational gaps into targeted document revisions. Rather than
performing unrestricted rewriting, QI-GEO generates struc-
tured edit specifications that identify what information should
be added and where it should be incorporated within the
document.
Each informational gap is transformed into an edit specifica-
tion consisting of three components: an anchor, a suggestion,
and a necessity score. The anchor identifies the sentence
or passage most closely related to the gap, the suggestion
describes the missing concept that should be incorporated,
and the necessity score reflects the importance of addressing
the gap. Anchoring edits to existing content provides a clear
location for modification and helps maintain consistency with
the surrounding context.
Edits are applied sequentially using the current version of
the document. To preserve document structure and minimize
unintended changes, the rewriter is instructed to make local-
ized additions rather than perform large-scale rewrites. In most
cases, edits are implemented by appending a short clause or
sentence to the selected anchor while leaving the remainder
of the document unchanged.
The use of anchored edits improves traceability throughout
the optimization process. Every revision can be linked back to
a specific informational gap and a corresponding location in
the original document, making the resulting changes easier to
inspect and verify.
The final output is an optimized document that incorporates
high-value missing information while preserving the intent,
structure, and content of the original text.
V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
A. Research Questions
The experiments are designed to evaluate whether docu-
ment semantics can be used as an alternative to query-based
```

```text
optimization in generative search engines. Specifically, we
investigate the following research questions:
• RQ1: Can user intent be inferred directly from a docu-
ment without access to explicit user queries?
• RQ2: Can semantic expansion reveal missing but relevant
information that improves document visibility in genera-
tive search engines?
• RQ3: Do the visibility gains achieved through query-
independent optimization remain consistent across differ-
ent formulations of the same information need?
B. Datasets and Benchmarks
Experiments are conducted using GEO-Bench [5] and Ex-
tendedGEOBench [6]. GEO-Bench is the standard benchmark
for evaluating visibility in generative search engines and
contains 10,000 query-document instances spanning a diverse
set of domains. Each query is associated with a fixed retrieval
pool consisting of five candidate documents and a designated
target document for optimization.
To evaluate robustness under query variation, we addition-
ally use ExtendedGEOBench [6], which groups semantically
related queries that express the same information need through
different phrasings. This benchmark makes it possible to
evaluate whether an optimization method remains effective
across multiple formulations of a topic rather than a single
query.
Following prior GEO work [5], [6], [8], all experiments use
a fixed-retrieval setting where the candidate document pool
remains unchanged throughout evaluation. This isolates the
effect of document modifications from retrieval variability and
ensures that changes in visibility can be attributed solely to the
optimization process.
For each query, the target document provided by the bench-
mark is optimized using QI-GEO and evaluated against its
original version while keeping the remaining documents in
the retrieval pool unchanged.
C. Experimental Configuration
QI-GEO is instantiated using a relation extraction, knowl-
edge graph expansion, and LLM-based rewriting pipeline.
Since the quality of extracted relations directly affects down-
stream expansion and gap discovery, we evaluate multiple
relation extractors including REBEL [10], RELiK [11], spaCy
[12], and an LLM-based extractor built using Qwen2.5 [13].
REBEL is used for all reported results because it consis-
tently produced the most useful triplets for knowledge graph
expansion. Its relation vocabulary is naturally aligned with
knowledge graph properties, resulting in more reliable entity
linking and downstream expansion.
Extracted triplets are linked to a knowledge graph and
expanded using one-hop neighborhood retrieval. To keep
expansion focused on concepts that are directly related to
the document, generic and metadata-oriented relations are
filtered while definitional, explanatory, and causal relations
are retained. Candidate concepts are then ranked using the
convergence-based scoring strategy described in Section IV
and filtered using semantic similarity and coverage checks.
Selected informational gaps are converted into edit requests
and incorporated into the document using Qwen2.5 7B [13].
Rewriting is performed through localized edits anchored to
existing document content so that missing information can be
introduced without substantially altering the original structure
or meaning of the document.
D. Evaluation Metrics
We evaluate QI-GEO using objective, subjective, and sta-
bility metrics that are commonly used in GEO research.
Objective metrics: We report Word Count Impression
(WC), Position Impression (PI), and Position-Adjusted Word
Count (PAWC) [5]. WC measures the proportion of generated
content attributed to a document, while PI measures how
prominently that content appears based on citation position.
PAWC combines these two signals by weighting word contri-
butions according to their position in the response, assigning
greater importance to citations that appear earlier.

where Sci is the set of sentences citing document ci and Sr
is the set of all sentences in the response. If a sentence contains
multiple citations, the contribution is divided equally among
the cited sources. Since PAWC captures both citation volume
and citation prominence, it is used as the primary objective
metric throughout this work.
Subjective metrics: We also report subjective impression
scores following the GEO evaluation framework [5]. These
scores estimate how visible and influential a document ap-
pears from a user perspective. The evaluation considers seven
dimensions: relevance, influence, uniqueness, diversity, click
follow-up likelihood, subjective position, and subjective vol-
ume. Each dimension is scored on a five-point scale, and the
final subjective score is computed as the average across all
dimensions.
Stability metrics: To evaluate robustness across query
variations, we report Mean Gain, Win-Tie Rate (WTR), Worst-
Case Performance (WCP), and Downside Risk (DR) [8]. Mean
Gain measures the average relative improvement over the
original document. WTR measures the fraction of queries for
which the optimized document performs at least as well as the
original. WCP reports the largest observed performance drop
across all evaluated queries, while DR measures the magnitude
of negative outcomes. Together, these metrics provide a more
complete picture of optimization reliability beyond average
performance alone.
```

```text
VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
This paper introduced Query-Implied Optimization (QI-
GEO), a query-independent framework for Generative Engine
Optimization. Existing GEO methods typically rely on explicit
queries or query-derived signals to guide document optimiza-
tion. In contrast, QI-GEO models user intent directly from
document semantics. By extracting entities and relationships,
expanding them through a knowledge graph, and identifying
informational gaps, QI-GEO discovers concepts that may be
relevant to user information needs without requiring access to
future queries.
Experiments on GEO-Bench and ExtendedGEOBench show
that QI-GEO improves citation coverage, source visibility,
and subjective impression scores compared to the original
documents. The results further demonstrate that these im-
provements remain effective across semantically related query
variations, suggesting that document-centric intent modeling
can serve as a viable alternative to query-based optimization
strategies.
Several directions remain for future work. First, richer
knowledge graph expansion strategies could improve the qual-
ity and coverage of discovered informational gaps. Second,
future systems could jointly model multiple inferred intents
during optimization rather than treating candidate gaps in-
dependently. Finally, while this work uses a general-purpose
knowledge graph, domain-specific knowledge graphs may pro-
vide more precise semantic relationships and enable stronger
optimization in specialized domains such as law, finance,
healthcare, and geospatial information. These directions offer
promising opportunities for improving the effectiveness and
generality of query-independent GEO systems.
```
